metadata.transformation_policy: Preserve concepts, mechanisms, purposes, examples, historical relationships, distinctions, references and source context. Do not silently correct or replace source claims.
metadata.core_thesis: An operating system is system software that manages computer hardware/software resources and provides common services, while mediating hardware access, isolating applications, abstracting hardware, scheduling execution, managing memory/I/O, and providing security and portability mechanisms.
metadata.relationship_policy: Relationships are directional and mechanism-bearing where possible. Rich edges preserve mechanism, effect, conditions, inverse/converse, scope and architectural context.

nodes.definition: System software managing computer hardware/software resources and providing common services for programs.

nodes.label: Source claim 1
nodes.statement: An operating system manages computer hardware/software resources and provides common services for computer programs.

nodes.label: Source claim 2
nodes.statement: Time-sharing OSes schedule tasks for efficient system use and may account for resource consumption.

nodes.label: Source claim 3
nodes.statement: OS acts as an intermediary for input/output and memory allocation while application code usually executes directly on hardware.

nodes.label: Source claim 4
nodes.statement: OS resource allocation shares CPU time/memory and prevents one program monopolizing limited hardware.

nodes.label: Source claim 5
nodes.statement: OS isolates applications to protect against errors/security vulnerabilities while enabling communication.

nodes.label: Source claim 6
nodes.statement: OS abstracts hardware access and virtualization can mask limited hardware resources.

nodes.label: Source claim 7
nodes.statement: OS common services for network/disk access enable applications to run across different hardware.

nodes.label: Source claim 8
nodes.statement: Multicomputers have multiple CPUs with separate memory and need efficient communication.

nodes.label: Source claim 9
nodes.statement: Distributed systems consist of distinct networked computers that may have their own OS/filesystem; middleware can improve consistency.

nodes.label: Source claim 10
nodes.statement: Embedded OSes target embedded systems and may omit application protection when no user-installed software is loaded.

nodes.label: Source claim 11
nodes.statement: Hard real-time systems require exact timing; soft real-time permits occasional missed events.

nodes.label: Source claim 12
nodes.statement: Hypervisors run VMs that emulate hardware and support OS research/development/debugging and portability.

nodes.label: Source claim 13
nodes.statement: Library OS services can be composed into a specialized single-address-space unikernel.

nodes.label: Source claim 14
nodes.statement: Early computers were directly programmed without OSes; operators manually performed scheduling/resource-management tasks.

nodes.label: Source claim 15
nodes.statement: OS/360 popularized multiprogramming and required memory partitioning and safeguards.

nodes.label: Source claim 16
nodes.statement: MULTICS targeted hundreds of simultaneous users; UNIX originated as a single-user development of MULTICS.

nodes.label: Source claim 17
nodes.statement: UNIX source availability led to System V and BSD; POSIX improved compatibility.

nodes.label: Source claim 18
nodes.statement: MINIX inspired Linux; MINIX later appeared in Intel microchip controllers.

nodes.label: Source claim 19

nodes.label: Source claim 20
nodes.statement: Macintosh popularized GUI; Windows evolved from a GUI overlay to standalone Windows NT.

nodes.label: Source claim 21
nodes.statement: Android became a major mobile OS, using a Linux kernel and Bionic C library.

nodes.label: Source claim 22
nodes.statement: Kernel protects applications/users, manages memory, controls I/O, and separates user/kernel privilege.

nodes.label: Source claim 23
nodes.statement: Program execution typically creates a process, assigns resources/priority, loads binary code and starts execution.

nodes.label: Source claim 24
nodes.statement: Interrupts transfer control to an ISR and require saving/restoring execution state.

nodes.label: Source claim 25
nodes.statement: Software interrupts can represent normal timing, errors, user messages, and process communication.

nodes.label: Source claim 26

nodes.label: Source claim 27

nodes.label: Source claim 28

nodes.label: Source claim 29

nodes.label: Source claim 30

nodes.label: OS vs kernel
nodes.description: Kernel is the always-running core; an OS can include system programs and other software beyond the kernel.

nodes.label: OS vs application
nodes.description: OS provides resource management/services; applications are other software running on the computer.

nodes.label: OS abstraction vs direct hardware execution
nodes.description: Application code generally executes directly on hardware but requests OS services and follows OS rules for privileged/hardware operations.

nodes.label: Multiprocessor vs multicomputer
nodes.description: Multiprocessors share memory; multicomputers have multiple CPUs with separate memory.

nodes.label: Multicomputer vs distributed system
nodes.description: Multicomputers are tightly coupled CPU/memory systems; distributed systems are distinct networked computers potentially dispersed worldwide.

nodes.label: Middleware vs OS
nodes.description: Middleware can function similarly to an OS but is an additional layer and not a true OS.

nodes.label: Embedded vs general purpose
nodes.description: Embedded systems may omit user-application protection because they do not load user-installed software.

nodes.label: Hard vs soft real-time
nodes.description: Hard real-time requires exact timing; soft real-time tolerates occasional missed events.

nodes.label: Hypervisor vs VM
nodes.description: The source describes the hypervisor as running a VM, while the VM is the application that emulates hardware.

nodes.label: Library OS vs conventional OS
nodes.description: libOS provides OS services as libraries composed with an application, reducing protection/context-switch overhead in the described single-application model.

nodes.label: User mode vs kernel mode
nodes.description: User mode is hardware-restricted; kernel mode has unrestricted OS privilege.

nodes.label: Hardware vs software interrupt
nodes.description: Hardware interrupt reports an event to the CPU; software interrupt communicates an event to a process/change of execution.

nodes.label: Interrupt vs signal
nodes.description: Signals are Unix-like process notifications analogous to software/hardware interrupt behavior but are an OS process communication mechanism.

nodes.label: Segmentation vs paging
nodes.description: Both provide memory protection, but they are distinct address-management mechanisms requiring hardware support.

nodes.label: Virtual memory vs physical memory
nodes.description: Virtual memory presents a logical address space whose backing can span RAM and disk rather than exposing physical layout directly.

nodes.label: Context switch vs interrupt
nodes.description: An interrupt can cause a context switch, but an interrupt is the event/control-transfer mechanism whereas a context switch changes the running process.

nodes.label: Resource allocation vs isolation
nodes.description: Allocation shares finite resources; isolation prevents one application's errors/authority from interfering with others.

nodes.label: Portability vs abstraction
nodes.description: Hardware abstraction and common OS services let applications run across different hardware without rewriting hardware-specific access.

nodes.label: UNIX vs POSIX
nodes.description: UNIX is an OS family/history; POSIX is an API standard for compatibility.

nodes.label: Linux vs Android
nodes.description: Android is closely based on Linux but uses a distinct user-space stack including Bionic and substantial Java code.

nodes.label: GUI vs CLI
nodes.description: GUI provides graphical interaction; CLI is text-based command interaction.

nodes.label: Preemptive vs cooperative behavior
nodes.description: Preemptive multitasking lets the OS scheduler interrupt/reassign CPU execution rather than relying entirely on voluntary cooperation.

nodes.label: System call vs library call
nodes.description: System calls request kernel services; libOS services can be accessed through simple library calls without usual context switches.

nodes.label: Protection vs no protection
nodes.description: Some specialized OS designs deliberately omit conventional application protection when their workload model makes it unnecessary.

nodes.label: An operating system is just the kernel.
nodes.correction: The source explicitly distinguishes the kernel from system programs and applications; an OS can include software beyond the kernel.

nodes.label: Applications never execute directly on hardware.
nodes.correction: The source says application code is usually executed directly by hardware while interacting with OS services through calls/interrupts.

nodes.label: OS abstraction means hardware is irrelevant.
nodes.correction: The OS abstracts hardware details, but the kernel, drivers and hardware privilege mechanisms still mediate execution.

nodes.label: Multicomputer and multiprocessor mean the same thing.
nodes.correction: Multiprocessors share memory; multicomputers have separate memory per CPU.

nodes.label: A distributed system is one giant computer.
nodes.correction: The source describes distinct networked computers, potentially dispersed worldwide, each with its own OS/filesystem.

nodes.label: All operating systems require full application isolation.
nodes.correction: Embedded and some hard-real-time/library OS designs may omit protection between applications under their workload assumptions.

nodes.label: Real-time means merely fast.
nodes.correction: Real-time is defined by timing guarantees/deadlines; hard real-time requires exact timing, not simply high throughput.

nodes.label: A VM is the same thing as a hypervisor.
nodes.correction: The source distinguishes the hypervisor from the VM it runs.

nodes.label: Virtual memory is the same as physical RAM.
nodes.correction: Virtual memory abstracts physical memory and can use scattered RAM and disk/backing storage.

nodes.label: Every interrupt is a context switch.
nodes.correction: An interrupt can cause a context switch; the interrupt itself is the event/control-transfer mechanism.

nodes.label: A software interrupt is a hardware interrupt.
nodes.correction: The source distinguishes software interrupts/messages to processes from hardware interrupts/messages to the CPU.

nodes.label: POSIX is a UNIX operating system.
nodes.correction: POSIX is an API standard intended to increase compatibility among UNIX systems.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: The OS decides when applications receive CPU time and how much memory/resources they receive.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Prevents a single application from monopolizing limited hardware and enables concurrent application execution.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Multiple applications contend for finite CPU and memory resources.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Without allocation, one program could monopolize resources.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: The OS separates applications so errors and security vulnerabilities in one application are contained while communication remains possible.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Improves reliability and security without eliminating application communication.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Isolation must coexist with controlled inter-application communication.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Unrestricted sharing increases interference risk.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: OS interfaces hide hardware-access details such as physical memory behind standardized services/interfaces.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Programmers can develop against OS abstractions rather than hardware-specific details.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Hardware differences remain beneath the abstraction.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Bypassing abstractions increases hardware dependence.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: OS exposes reusable interfaces for networking, disks and other common facilities.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Applications can run across different hardware without being rewritten for each hardware implementation.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Service set varies greatly between OS designs.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Missing services can force applications to depend on hardware-specific implementations.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Paging/segmentation let the kernel choose mappings and use disk/RAM as a larger logical memory space.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: A program can perceive a large continuous address space even when physical memory is scattered or limited.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Requires hardware support and OS memory-management mechanisms.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Invalid/restricted addresses can trigger faults.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Kernel-enforced protection separates applications/users and limits their resource authority.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Errors remain isolated and malicious software has less power to compromise private data or monopolize resources.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Depends on hardware privilege/memory-protection mechanisms.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Broken protection increases cross-process interference.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Hardware checks user-mode software for legal instructions while kernel mode has unrestricted powers.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Separates ordinary application execution from privileged OS control.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Requires processor support for privilege modes.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Executing privileged operations from user mode is prevented or traps to the kernel.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: The kernel creates a process, assigns memory/resources/priority, loads its binary and starts execution.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Turns an application program into a managed unit of execution.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Exact process model varies by OS.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: An application may also execute another application within the same process or via a separate thread in systems described.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: An interrupt changes CPU control flow to an interrupt service routine; state is saved and later restored.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Allows the OS to react efficiently to hardware/software events.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Architecture-specific interrupt handling differs.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: No interrupt handling would prevent timely OS reaction to device/events.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: When a device completes I/O it can interrupt the running process/CPU and provide status information.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: The OS can resume or schedule the process associated with the completed I/O.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Uses interrupt handlers, process state and context switching.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: If completion is not handled, the waiting process cannot be resumed normally.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: The scheduler changes the running process by saving one process's CPU state and restoring another's.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: CPU time is shared among runnable processes.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Depends on saved CPU state such as registers and program counter.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: A context switch is unnecessary when no process change occurs.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Hardware-supported segmentation or paging restricts which addresses a process may access.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: One process cannot normally overwrite another process's memory; invalid access triggers an interrupt/fault.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Requires hardware support such as an MMU.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: A faulty/malicious access can cause a segmentation violation and process termination.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Protected registers define permitted address regions; invalid access causes an interrupt and re-entry into supervisor mode.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: The kernel regains control and can terminate the offending program.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: The source describes segmentation violation as a common response.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Valid access avoids the fault.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: When one job waits for I/O, another job can use the CPU; multiple jobs are held in memory with partitioning and safeguards.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Improves CPU utilization while preventing one job from accessing another's memory.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Requires memory partitioning/protection.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Without multiprogramming, I/O wait would leave CPU less utilized.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: IEEE POSIX standardizes OS application-programming interfaces supported by most UNIX systems.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Applications gain a common API target across compatible UNIX systems.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: POSIX is an API compatibility standard, not an operating system.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Nonstandard APIs reduce portability.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: OS services are provided as libraries and composed with one application/configuration code into a specialized single-address-space image.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Avoids usual context-switch overhead and can deploy a minimal machine image.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Single application means traditional inter-application protection domains are unnecessary in the described model.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: More conventional OS boundaries reintroduce mode/context-switch overhead.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Mode switching can pollute important processor structures including caches and the instruction pipeline.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: System-call/mode-switch overhead can reduce user- and kernel-mode performance beyond direct switching cost.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: The cited FlexSC discussion emphasizes both direct and indirect costs.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Avoiding or reducing mode switches can reduce this source of overhead.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Remote direct memory access permits one CPU to access memory belonging to another CPU.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Reduces reliance on packet copying for cross-CPU data movement.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Architecture/network support is required.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Without RDMA, explicit communication/copying mechanisms are used.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Middleware sits between OS and applications and is used to improve consistency across distinct networked computers.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Provides a higher-level coordination layer without becoming the OS.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Each participating computer can retain its own OS and filesystem.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Middleware is not itself a true OS.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Hard real-time systems require exact processing by or at specified moments.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Missed deadlines are unacceptable in the intended timing model.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Common in manufacturing, avionics and military uses per source.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Soft real-time permits occasional missed events.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Soft real-time accepts occasional missed events.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Supports workloads such as audio/multimedia and smartphones where occasional deadline misses are acceptable.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Timing guarantee is weaker than hard real-time.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Hard real-time does not permit the same relaxation.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Windows uses ACLs, integrity levels, process authentication tokens and object security descriptors.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Controls access to objects and processes and strengthens OS security.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Later releases add further security features.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Removing access controls broadens authority.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Android is closely based on Linux and uses a Linux kernel with Bionic.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Provides a Linux-derived OS foundation for mobile and embedded systems.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Much Android code is written in Java and uses object-oriented design.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: The Android user-space stack differs from a conventional Linux distribution.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Linux is written in C according to the source.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Provides a low-level systems implementation foundation.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: The source also describes UNIX-compatible syntax/networking and multiple-user preemptive multitasking.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Different language choices would change implementation properties but not the OS abstraction itself.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: VMs can be paused, saved and resumed and can emulate hardware for an OS.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Useful for OS research, development and debugging, while improving portability.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: The VM acts as an application emulating hardware.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Without virtualization, incompatible applications may require compatible base OS/hardware.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Embedded systems described do not load user-installed software, so they may not need protection between applications.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Permits very small/simple OS designs.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Applies to the embedded systems described in the source.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: General-purpose user-installed software would create stronger isolation requirements.

source_claims.statement: An operating system manages computer hardware/software resources and provides common services for computer programs.
Time-sharing OSes schedule tasks for efficient system use and may account for resource consumption.
OS acts as an intermediary for input/output and memory allocation while application code usually executes directly on hardware.
OS resource allocation shares CPU time/memory and prevents one program monopolizing limited hardware.
OS isolates applications to protect against errors/security vulnerabilities while enabling communication.
OS abstracts hardware access and virtualization can mask limited hardware resources.
OS common services for network/disk access enable applications to run across different hardware.
Multicomputers have multiple CPUs with separate memory and need efficient communication.
Distributed systems consist of distinct networked computers that may have their own OS/filesystem; middleware can improve consistency.
Embedded OSes target embedded systems and may omit application protection when no user-installed software is loaded.
Hard real-time systems require exact timing; soft real-time permits occasional missed events.
Hypervisors run VMs that emulate hardware and support OS research/development/debugging and portability.
Library OS services can be composed into a specialized single-address-space unikernel.
Early computers were directly programmed without OSes; operators manually performed scheduling/resource-management tasks.
OS/360 popularized multiprogramming and required memory partitioning and safeguards.
MULTICS targeted hundreds of simultaneous users; UNIX originated as a single-user development of MULTICS.
UNIX source availability led to System V and BSD; POSIX improved compatibility.
MINIX inspired Linux; MINIX later appeared in Intel microchip controllers.
CP/M was popular on early microcomputers; MS-DOS/IBM PC DOS became widespread on IBM PC compatibles.
Macintosh popularized GUI; Windows evolved from a GUI overlay to standalone Windows NT.
Android became a major mobile OS, using a Linux kernel and Bionic C library.
Kernel protects applications/users, manages memory, controls I/O, and separates user/kernel privilege.
Program execution typically creates a process, assigns resources/priority, loads binary code and starts execution.
Interrupts transfer control to an ISR and require saving/restoring execution state.
Software interrupts can represent normal timing, errors, user messages, and process communication.
Unix signals communicate asynchronous events; pipes coordinate producer/consumer processes.
Memory protection uses hardware-supported segmentation/paging; invalid access can trigger a segmentation violation.
Virtual memory can map scattered RAM/disk storage into a logical continuous address space.
Windows uses NTFS, Windows Driver Model, demand paging, preemptive scheduling, ACLs, integrity levels, authentication tokens and security descriptors.
Linux is distributed under GPL, uses a kernel/libraries/utilities structure, supports UNIX networking and preemptive multitasking, and can operate from small systems to large multiprocessors.

semantic_distinctions.description: OS provides resource management/services; applications are other software running on the computer.

semantic_distinctions.label: OS abstraction vs direct hardware execution
semantic_distinctions.description: Application code generally executes directly on hardware but requests OS services and follows OS rules for privileged/hardware operations.

semantic_distinctions.label: Multiprocessor vs multicomputer
semantic_distinctions.description: Multiprocessors share memory; multicomputers have multiple CPUs with separate memory.

semantic_distinctions.label: Multicomputer vs distributed system
semantic_distinctions.description: Multicomputers are tightly coupled CPU/memory systems; distributed systems are distinct networked computers potentially dispersed worldwide.

semantic_distinctions.label: Middleware vs OS
semantic_distinctions.description: Middleware can function similarly to an OS but is an additional layer and not a true OS.

semantic_distinctions.label: Embedded vs general purpose
semantic_distinctions.description: Embedded systems may omit user-application protection because they do not load user-installed software.

semantic_distinctions.label: Hard vs soft real-time
semantic_distinctions.description: Hard real-time requires exact timing; soft real-time tolerates occasional missed events.

semantic_distinctions.label: Hypervisor vs VM
semantic_distinctions.description: The source describes the hypervisor as running a VM, while the VM is the application that emulates hardware.

semantic_distinctions.label: Library OS vs conventional OS
semantic_distinctions.description: libOS provides OS services as libraries composed with an application, reducing protection/context-switch overhead in the described single-application model.

semantic_distinctions.label: User mode vs kernel mode
semantic_distinctions.description: User mode is hardware-restricted; kernel mode has unrestricted OS privilege.

semantic_distinctions.label: Hardware vs software interrupt
semantic_distinctions.description: Hardware interrupt reports an event to the CPU; software interrupt communicates an event to a process/change of execution.

semantic_distinctions.label: Interrupt vs signal
semantic_distinctions.description: Signals are Unix-like process notifications analogous to software/hardware interrupt behavior but are an OS process communication mechanism.

semantic_distinctions.label: Segmentation vs paging
semantic_distinctions.description: Both provide memory protection, but they are distinct address-management mechanisms requiring hardware support.

semantic_distinctions.label: Virtual memory vs physical memory
semantic_distinctions.description: Virtual memory presents a logical address space whose backing can span RAM and disk rather than exposing physical layout directly.

semantic_distinctions.label: Context switch vs interrupt
semantic_distinctions.description: An interrupt can cause a context switch, but an interrupt is the event/control-transfer mechanism whereas a context switch changes the running process.

semantic_distinctions.label: Resource allocation vs isolation
semantic_distinctions.description: Allocation shares finite resources; isolation prevents one application's errors/authority from interfering with others.

semantic_distinctions.label: Portability vs abstraction
semantic_distinctions.description: Hardware abstraction and common OS services let applications run across different hardware without rewriting hardware-specific access.

semantic_distinctions.label: UNIX vs POSIX
semantic_distinctions.description: UNIX is an OS family/history; POSIX is an API standard for compatibility.

semantic_distinctions.label: Linux vs Android
semantic_distinctions.description: Android is closely based on Linux but uses a distinct user-space stack including Bionic and substantial Java code.

semantic_distinctions.label: GUI vs CLI
semantic_distinctions.description: GUI provides graphical interaction; CLI is text-based command interaction.

semantic_distinctions.label: Preemptive vs cooperative behavior
semantic_distinctions.description: Preemptive multitasking lets the OS scheduler interrupt/reassign CPU execution rather than relying entirely on voluntary cooperation.

semantic_distinctions.label: System call vs library call
semantic_distinctions.description: System calls request kernel services; libOS services can be accessed through simple library calls without usual context switches.

semantic_distinctions.label: Protection vs no protection
semantic_distinctions.description: Some specialized OS designs deliberately omit conventional application protection when their workload model makes it unnecessary.

misconceptions.statement: An operating system is just the kernel.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly distinguishes the kernel from system programs and applications; an OS can include software beyond the kernel.

misconceptions.statement: Applications never execute directly on hardware.
misconceptions.correction: The source says application code is usually executed directly by hardware while interacting with OS services through calls/interrupts.

misconceptions.statement: OS abstraction means hardware is irrelevant.
misconceptions.correction: The OS abstracts hardware details, but the kernel, drivers and hardware privilege mechanisms still mediate execution.

misconceptions.statement: Multicomputer and multiprocessor mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Multiprocessors share memory; multicomputers have separate memory per CPU.

misconceptions.statement: A distributed system is one giant computer.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes distinct networked computers, potentially dispersed worldwide, each with its own OS/filesystem.

misconceptions.statement: All operating systems require full application isolation.
misconceptions.correction: Embedded and some hard-real-time/library OS designs may omit protection between applications under their workload assumptions.
Real-time is defined by timing guarantees/deadlines; hard real-time requires exact timing, not simply high throughput.

misconceptions.statement: A VM is the same thing as a hypervisor.
misconceptions.correction: The source distinguishes the hypervisor from the VM it runs.

misconceptions.statement: Virtual memory is the same as physical RAM.
misconceptions.correction: Virtual memory abstracts physical memory and can use scattered RAM and disk/backing storage.

misconceptions.statement: Every interrupt is a context switch.
misconceptions.correction: An interrupt can cause a context switch; the interrupt itself is the event/control-transfer mechanism.

misconceptions.statement: A software interrupt is a hardware interrupt.
misconceptions.correction: The source distinguishes software interrupts/messages to processes from hardware interrupts/messages to the CPU.

misconceptions.statement: POSIX is a UNIX operating system.
misconceptions.correction: POSIX is an API standard intended to increase compatibility among UNIX systems.
